kaps_punt: Handel as ruil van goedere; en Handel as die koop en verkoop van goedere vir geld

items.bewering: 'n Boer plant mielies op sy plaas maar hy maak nie self skoene nie.
items.bron: St. Louis Fed, Economic Education 'Tools for Teaching' Session 14 (https://www.stlouisfed.org/-/media/project/frbstl/stlouisfed/education/tools/pdf/ea-tools-for-teaching-session-14.pdf): individuals specialise in producing some goods and services and obtain the rest through trade. The farmer-who-does-not-make-shoes example is an ordinary instance of that specialisation.

items.bewering: Niemand kan alles wat hy nodig het self maak, plant of myn nie.
items.bron: St. Louis Fed Session 14 (as above), and BLS Monthly Labor Review review of Kling, 'Specialization and Trade' (https://www.bls.gov/opub/mlr/2019/book-review/specialization-and-trade.htm): because skills, time and resources are limited, people specialise rather than produce everything they use. The universal 'niemand ... alles' is about an individual ('hy'), where it holds; whole communities have at times been close to self-sufficient, but the sentence does not claim anything about communities.

items.bewering: Baie mense maak of plant meestal een ding, meer as wat hulle nodig het. Van ander dinge het hulle te min.
items.bron: St. Louis Fed Session 14; BLS review of Kling (as above): specialists produce more of their specialty than they need and exchange the surplus for what they have not produced. 'Baie mense' and 'meestal' are suitably hedged.

items.bewering: Die boer het baie mielies en die visser by die see het sout.
items.bron: The mapping is the fault, not the sentence taken alone. The block's principle, in the sentence before, is that each person makes or grows mostly ONE thing in surplus; the example then pairs the farmer with what his work produces (maize) and the fisher with something his work does not produce (salt). Salt is made by evaporating brine at salt works and salt pans, a separate occupation (Historic England, 'Pre-industrial Salterns', https://historicengland.org.uk/images-books/publications/iha-preindustrial-salterns/heag225-pre-industrial-salterns/; Gittins 2005 on the bay-salt trade, https://www.gwern.net/doc/economics/2005-gittins.pdf), and historically fishers were BUYERS of salt to preserve their catch: the fish trade depended on imported salt, and early Atlantic fishing fleets carried shiploads of salt out with them (Gittins; Fishermen's Voice, 'Got salt?', https://www.fishermensvoice.com/archives/0408gotsalt.html). In southern Africa salt was collected at pans such as those inland (SAHRA heritage report, https://sahris.sahra.org.za/sites/default/files/heritagereports/9-2-013-0003-19980801-ACO_0.pdf), not produced by fishing. Some coastal people did make salt, so a fisher owning salt is not impossible; but a learner reasoning from this example learns that a fisher's work yields salt, which inverts the real relationship and undercuts the lesson's own point that a person's surplus is what their own work produces. The same pairing carries into the blocks 'Ruil sonder geld', 'Wanneer 'n direkte ruil moeilik raak' and 'Koop en verkoop met geld'.
items.regstelling: Give the salt to a person whose work makes salt, so that each person's surplus is what their own work produces: for example someone at the coast or at a salt pan who makes salt (a soutmaker), in place of the fisher. Keeping salt as the traded good leaves the rest of the story intact; the person who supplies it must change in every block where the fisher appears. Whatever wording is chosen, do not keep a fisher whose surplus is salt.

items.bewering: Uit hierdie verskil tussen mense ontstaan handel.
items.bron: St. Louis Fed Session 14: people trade because each receives something they value more than what they give up, which presupposes that they hold different things; BLS review of Kling: specialisation and differences in skills and resources are the basis of trade.

items.bewering: Die boer neem sy mielies na die visser en kry sout terug.
items.bron: As an illustration of a direct goods-for-goods exchange this is barter as Britannica defines it (https://www.britannica.com/money/barter-trade). Note that the trading partner inherits the mapping fault reported under 'Die boer het baie mielies en die visser by die see het sout'.

items.bewering: Handel is wanneer mense goedere of dienste uitruil: deur te ruil, of deur te koop en te verkoop.
items.bron: EIONET GEMET thesaurus, 'trade': the act or process of buying, selling or exchanging commodities (https://www.eionet.europa.eu/gemet/nl/concept/8566); Britannica Money places barter within commerce (https://www.britannica.com/money/barter-trade). Dutch/Afrikaans 'handel' covers buying, selling and exchange (DSAE entry 'handel', https://dsae.co.za/entry/handel/e02910). No authoritative Afrikaans dictionary entry (WAT/HAT) surfaced online; the definition rests on the English and Dutch sources, which agree.

items.bewering: Ruilhandel is die naam vir hierdie direkte ruil sonder geld.
items.bron: Britannica Money, 'barter': direct trade of goods or services without the use of money (https://www.britannica.com/money/barter-trade); EuroVoc pairs Dutch 'ruilhandel' with English 'barter' (https://light.onki.fi/eurovoc/en/page/4573?clang=da).

items.bewering: Ruilhandel is een manier om handel te dryf en nie 'n ander naam vir handel nie.
items.bron: Britannica Money describes barter as a form of commerce, i.e. one kind of trade (https://www.britannica.com/money/barter-trade); GEMET defines trade as buying, selling OR exchanging, so barter is a subset (https://www.eionet.europa.eu/gemet/nl/concept/8566).

items.bewering: Die visser moet mielies wil hê op dieselfde dag dat die boer sout soek. Wil hy daardie dag iets anders hê, loop die boer met sy sak weg.
items.bron: IMF Finance & Development, 'Back to Basics: What Is Money?' (Asmundson and Oner, 2012, https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/2012/09/basics.htm): under barter every item must be exchanged for something the other person can provide and wants (the mechanic who must find a farmer whose car needs repair) - the double coincidence of wants. The timing element is a fair rendering of it.

items.bewering: Baie goedere kan ook nie in kleiner stukke verdeel word nie. Jy kan nie 'n halwe bok vir 'n handvol sout aanbied nie.
items.bron: Encyclopedia.com, 'Barter' (https://encyclopedia.com/law/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/barter) and standard economics treatments: indivisibility of goods such as livestock is a recognised difficulty of barter; a live animal cannot be halved. The lesson says this makes direct exchange difficult, not impossible, which is the accurate framing (traders could work around it with extra goods or credit).

items.bewering: Vis en melk bly ook nie lank goed nie en raak gou sleg.
items.bron: Fish: Torry Advisory Note No. 1 hosted by FAO, 'fish is a highly perishable foodstuff' (https://www.fao.org/4/x5882e/x5882e00.htm); review in Foods 2021, fresh fish has a short shelf life (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8066737/). Milk: FAO milk-cooling guidance requires raw milk to be cooled within hours of milking to limit spoilage (FAO 2016 technical and investment guidelines for milk cooling centres, cited at https://qftp.org/wp-content/archive/en/3-14-E~1.PDF). IMF 'What Is Money?' uses perishables as the example of goods that cannot be saved for later trade.

items.bewering: Geld beteken die koper en die verkoper hoef nie meer presies by mekaar te pas nie.
items.bron: IMF 'What Is Money?' (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/2012/09/basics.htm): with money you sell to anyone and buy from anyone who accepts the same money, so no particular trading partner is needed. Mapping checked: the lesson tells barter, then its difficulties, then money, and 'nie meer' could lead a learner to infer that money was historically invented to replace a barter economy. That origin story is contested - anthropology finds no pure barter economy from which money emerged (Humphrey 1985, as discussed at https://www.historynewsnetwork.org/article/162141 and https://era.org.au/money-and-the-myth-of-barter/), while Britannica calls barter the oldest form of commerce. The lesson itself makes no historical claim: 'nie meer' sits inside one farmer's story, and the list block states that barter continues today, which works against a strict sequence. The functional claim stands as written. Do not add a sentence saying money was invented because barter was difficult.

items.bewering: Die boer verkoop sy mielies aan enigeen wat mielies nodig het. Hy koop dan met daardie geld sout by 'n heel ander mens.
items.bron: IMF 'What Is Money?' (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/2012/09/basics.htm): money as a medium of exchange - sell in a market, then buy from anyone who accepts the same money.

items.bewering: Geld werk omdat die mense rondom jou dit as betaling aanvaar.
items.bron: IMF 'What Is Money?' (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/2012/09/basics.htm): 'money works because people believe that it will'; fiat money has value because a nation collectively agrees to ascribe value to it; 'If it is accepted as money, it is money.'

items.bewering: Hy kan die geld ook hou tot hy iets anders nodig het.
items.bron: IMF 'What Is Money?' (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/2012/09/basics.htm): money is a store of value - people can save it and use it later. (Inflation erodes it over time, which the sentence does not deny.)

items.bewering: Met geld betaal mense ook vir dienste, soos wanneer 'n haarkapper jou hare sny.
items.bron: A haircut is the standard example of a service (an intangible act performed for the customer, delivered and consumed at once); Kotler's service definition as quoted in services-marketing course notes (https://forum.daffodilvarsity.edu.bd/index.php/topic,8293.0.html). IRS barter guidance likewise treats work such as landscaping and plumbing as services paid for (https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/bartering-produces-taxable-income-and-reporting-requirements).

items.bewering: Mense ruil vandag nog goedere en dienste direk vir mekaar sonder geld.
items.bron: IRS, 'Bartering produces taxable income and reporting requirements' (https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/bartering-produces-taxable-income-and-reporting-requirements): some businesses barter for products or services they need, individuals trade services directly, and barter exchanges operate, some online. South Africa: the tax court in South Atlantic Jazz Festival v CSARS treated sponsorship deals as barter (Webber Wentzel commentary, https://polity.org.za/article/uneven-barter-transactions-2022-11-22).

items.bewering: Mense koop en verkoop ook elke dag goedere met geld.
items.bron: IMF 'What Is Money?' (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/2012/09/basics.htm): money is what people use to buy and sell from one another; daily monetary purchasing is the normal case in a money economy.

items.bewering: Handel begin nie by geld nie maar by iets wat iemand nodig het.
items.bron: St. Louis Fed Session 14 (https://www.stlouisfed.org/-/media/project/frbstl/stlouisfed/education/tools/pdf/ea-tools-for-teaching-session-14.pdf): people trade to obtain what they value more than what they give up, i.e. trade is driven by wants, with money as the medium rather than the cause. Read as a conceptual statement this is sound; it makes no dated historical claim.

items.bewering: Handel is wanneer mense goedere of dienste uitruil: deur te ruil, of deur te koop en te verkoop.
items.bron: Same sentence as in 'Ruil sonder geld'; GEMET 'trade' (https://www.eionet.europa.eu/gemet/nl/concept/8566); Britannica Money 'barter' (https://www.britannica.com/money/barter-trade). The glossary entry and the study text agree word for word.

items.bewering: Ruilhandel is wanneer mense goedere of dienste direk vir mekaar ruil sonder geld.
items.bron: Britannica Money, 'barter': direct trade of goods or services without money (https://www.britannica.com/money/barter-trade); IRS: 'the trading of one product or service for another' (https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/bartering-produces-taxable-income-and-reporting-requirements).

items.bewering: Goedere is dinge wat mense ruil, koop of verkoop, soos mielies of skoene.
items.bron: Goods are tangible products that satisfy wants and can change hands (services-marketing definitions summarised at https://forum.daffodilvarsity.edu.bd/index.php/topic,8293.0.html; Britannica Money on barter of goods). Maize and shoes are correct examples. Defining goods by exchange rather than by tangibility is a simplification, not a falsehood: anything that can be traded as an object fits.

items.bewering: 'n Diens is werk wat iemand vir 'n ander doen, sodat die ander die werk self kry en nie 'n ding wat hy of sy kan hou nie.
items.bron: Kotler's definition of a service, quoted in services-marketing course notes (https://forum.daffodilvarsity.edu.bd/index.php/topic,8293.0.html): an act or performance that is essentially intangible and does not result in the ownership of anything. 'Nie 'n ding wat hy of sy kan hou nie' is a fair Grade 6 rendering of 'no transfer of ownership'. Edge cases where a service leaves a physical result (a builder, a tailor) are outside what this definition needs to handle.

opsomming: One fault, in the lesson's central example: the fisher's surplus is salt, which makes a fisher's work produce salt when salt comes from salt works and pans and fishers historically bought it to preserve their catch - give the salt to someone who makes salt; everything else, including the barter difficulties, the functions of money and all four definitions, checks out, and the lesson rightly avoids claiming that money was invented to replace barter, which is a contested origin story.
